articles.title: How We Built x402 Payments for AI Agents on Base Mainnet
articles.excerpt: From an HTTP 402 response to on-chain USDC in a few lines of code — with TypeScript and Python SDKs, dynamic commissions, and subscription tiers. AI agents need to pay for things: data APIs, compute,…
articles.body: From an HTTP 402 response to on-chain USDC in a few lines of code — with TypeScript and Python SDKs, dynamic commissions, and subscription tiers. AI agents need to pay for things: data APIs, compute, storage, and services provided by other agents. Traditional payment systems such as Stripe and PayPal are designed around human users. They require accounts, API keys, cards, approval flows, and sometimes KYC. That model does not work particularly well for autonomous software. x402 changes the interaction by turning HTTP 402 Payment Required into a crypto payment flow. An agent needs a wallet and a request. The server describes the payment requirements, the agent signs an authorization, and the payment is settled on-chain.

articles.body: Our laptop said 37 MB. The scoreboard said 195 MB . That was the first of eight times in 72 hours that the live board told us we were wrong about our own code, and each time, being wrong taught us more than being right. It also moved us up. On November 1 our Track C solution sat 43rd of the 91 teams that had scored it, at K 23.9 while the leaders were between 41 and 47. A day later it was K 32.4, and our Track D build had reached #9 of 117 on the board. This post is about those corrections. Speed Demon 2026 is a 72-hour performance-engineering hackathon run by Hackathon Raptors . Four tracks each hand you a correct but naive Python program, and you make it as fast as you can without changing a byte of its output.

articles.body: In conflict-affected countries, education is rarely disrupted by a single event. Schools close after attacks, families move away, roads become unsafe, and teachers stop coming. Organisations trying to keep children learning have limited money and limited field staff, so they face a blunt question: Where is education access most likely to be disrupted, and where should we look first? I built the Mali Education Disruption Index (EDI) to give a first, data-driven answer to that question. It scores all 50 of Mali's cercles (the country's second-level administrative areas, roughly a district) and puts the result on an interactive map.

articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.

articles.body: Another new private rocket is in the works. The news comes just 10 days after Cowboy Space unveiled Big Iron , a rocket designed to launch its constellation of 20,000 AI data centers . Cowboy Space is also targeting 2028 for its first liftoff. "The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry," Abel Avellan, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, said in a statement today .

articles.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
articles.excerpt: Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.
articles.body: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky.

articles.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
articles.excerpt: Company said a "multifront cyberattack" included AI agents and an on-path data snatch.
articles.body: Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security. The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats. We regret to inform you...
